## Introduction: The Hidden State {.left auto-animate="true"}

::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="50%"}

::: {.fragment  .fade-in}
### Error is inescapable 
What is 5 cm truely? Can we ever measure a perfect 5cm?
:::
::: {.fragment  .fade-in}
### Yes and No
* To a drill press : 5cm => 5cm +- .5cm
* To a mill : 5cm => 5cm +- .005cm
* To an ASML Photolithography Machine: 5cm => 5cm +- 0.000002cm
:::

:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
::: {style="height: 5em;"}
:::
::: {.fragment .goal-box .fade-up}
### Today's Goal
The Mathmatics of finding truth through Error, and incorporating new data as Evidence rather than truth. 
Since by definition we cannot measure the error of any particular measurment, We use probability to model the likelyhood of sensing a true value
:::
::: {style="height: 2em;"}
:::
:::

:::



## Boolean vs. Probabilistic Logic
:::{.columns}
:::{.column width="50%"}
:::{.fragment}
### Boolean Logic

```{python}
#| echo: true
#| eval: false
# Boolean logic example
# if (Shooter_will_make_the_shot == True):
#     shoot
```


:::
:::{.fragment}
### Probabilistic Logic

```{python}
#| echo: true
#| eval: false
# Probability logic example
# if (Probability_we_make_the_shot >= 80%)
#     shoot
```

:::

:::
:::{.column width="50%"}
:::{.fragment}
### Key difference:
Combining evidence with trust levels enables better decisions.

* Boolean: Instantaneous sensor read → immediate judgment

* Probabilistic: Averages sensor noise, reduces false positives/negatives

:::
:::{.fragment}
### Caveat:
There are alternative filtering approaches that don't rely on probability:

- Rolling average on distance sensors
- Debounce period on limit switches  
- Moving median filters
- Exponential smoothing
- These can work very well depending on implementation and use case
:::
:::
::::

## Understanding Set Space {auto-animate=true data-autoslide="0"}
:::{.fragment}
- We want a number that represents how often something happens, or does not
:::
:::{.fragment}
- If you know nothing about an event, you could assume it's a 50:50 chance, pass or fail, it will happen or it wont
:::
:::{.fragment}
- With Evidence about the type of event (I.E. Rolling a 2 on a D6 Die) you can refine your guess, in this case to 1:6
:::
:::{.fragment}
- You can also experiment to find probability. If given a weighted die, you could roll it many times to gather data, and hone in on the true likelyhood of any given face landing up. 
:::

### Probability of Hitting The shot GIVEN the evidence the Shooter is broken
So what is P(Target Hit | Shooter was broken)?

</div>
<div data-id="label1" style="position: absolute; left: 150px; top: 550px; color: white; font-size: 40px;">$$P(\text{Target Hit} \cap \text{Shooter Broken})$$</div>
<!-- <div data-id="label1prob" style="position: absolute; left: 150px; top: 550px; color: white; font-size: 50px;">P(Target Hit AND Shooter Was Broken)</div> -->

<div data-id="label2" style="position: absolute;left: 700px; top: 40px; color: white; font-size: 50px; ">$$P(\text{Shooter Was Broken})$$</div>



<div data-id="eq" style="position: absolute;left: 150px; top: 750px; color: white; font-size: 30px; text-align: center;">
$$P(\text{Target Hit} \mid \text{Shooter Broken}) = \frac{P(\text{Target Hit} \cap \text{Shooter Broken})}{P(\text{Shooter Broken})}$$
</div>

:::
<!-- Slide 5: Understanding Set Space (Part 3 - AND) -->
## Understanding Set Space {auto-animate=true data-autoslide="0"}
### Bayes Theorem

::: {style="position: relative; width: 1500px; height: 880px; margin: auto;"}


<div data-id="eq" style="position: absolute;left: 50px; top: 200px; color: white; font-size: 30px; text-align: center; width: 95%;">
$$P(\text{Target Hit} \mid \text{Shooter Broken}) = \frac{P(\text{Target Hit} \cap \text{Shooter Broken})}{P(\text{Shooter Broken})}$$
</div>
<div data-id="eq2" style="position: absolute;left: 50px; top: 350px; color: white; font-size: 30px; text-align: center; width: 95%;">
$$P(\text{Shooter Broken}) = \frac{P(\text{Target Hit} \cap \text{Shooter Broken})}{P(\text{Target Hit} \mid \text{Shooter Broken})}$$
</div>
<div data-id="eq3" style="position: absolute;left: 50px; top: 500px; color: white; font-size: 30px; text-align: center; width: 95%;">
$$P(\text{Target Hit} \cap \text{Shooter Broken}) = P(\text{Shooter Broken}) \times P(\text{Target Hit} \mid \text{Shooter Broken})$$
</div>

:::
<!-- Slide 5: Understanding Set Space (Part 3 - AND) -->
## Understanding Set Space {auto-animate=true data-autoslide="0"}
### Bayes Theorem -- Generally

::: {style="position: relative; width: 1500px; height: 880px; margin: auto;"}


<div data-id="eq" style="position: absolute;left: 50px; top: 200px; color: white; font-size: 30px; text-align: center; width: 95%;">
$$P(\text{Event} \mid \text{Evidence}) = \frac{P(\text{Event} \cap \text{Evidence})}{P(\text{Evidence})}$$
</div>
<div data-id="eq2" style="position: absolute;left: 50px; top: 350px; color: white; font-size: 30px; text-align: center; width: 95%;">
$$P(\text{Evidence}) = \frac{P(\text{Event} \cap \text{Evidence})}{P(\text{Event} \mid \text{Evidence})}$$
</div>
<div data-id="eq3" style="position: absolute;left: 50px; top: 500px; color: white; font-size: 30px; text-align: center; width: 95%;">
$$P(\text{Event} \cap \text{Evidence}) = P(\text{Evidence}) \times P(\text{Event} \mid \text{Evidence})$$
</div>

:::
<!-- Slide 5: Understanding Set Space (Part 3 - AND) -->
## Understanding Set Space {auto-animate=true data-autoslide="0"}
### Bayes Theorem -- Generally
For events that are dependent, finding The intersection (AND) can be difficult. So Bayes tells us =>

::: {style="position: relative; width: 1500px; height: 880px; margin: auto;"}



<div data-id="eq3" style="position: absolute;left: 50px; top: 100px; color: white; font-size: 30px; text-align: center; width: 95%;">
$$P(\text{Evidence} \cap \text{Event}) = P(\text{Event}) \times P(\text{Evidence} \mid \text{Event})$$
</div>
<div data-id="eqtext" style="position: absolute;left: 50px; top: 300px; color: white; font-size: 60px; text-align: center; width: 95%;">
So we substitute and rewrite the our original equation as:
</div>

<div data-id="eq4" style="position: absolute;left: 50px; top: 500px; color: white; font-size: 30px; text-align: center; width: 95%;">
$$P(\text{Event} \mid \text{Evidence}) = \frac{P(\text{Event}) \times P(\text{Evidence} \mid \text{Event})}{P(\text{Evidence})}$$
</div>


:::

<!-- Slide 5: Understanding Set Space (Part 3 - AND) -->
## Understanding Set Space {auto-animate=true data-autoslide="0"}
### Bayes Theorem -- Generally
For events that are dependent, finding The intersection (AND) can be difficult. So Bayes tells us =>

::: {style="position: relative; width: 1500px; height: 880px; margin: auto;"}


<div data-id="eq4" style="position: absolute;left: 50px; top: 10px; color: white; font-size: 30px; text-align: center; width: 95%;">
$$P(\text{Event} \mid \text{Evidence}) = \frac{P(\text{Event}) \times \text{Likelihood of this evidence given the event happening}}{P(\text{Evidence})}$$
</div>

<div data-id="explanation" style="position: absolute;left: 50px; top: 200px; color: #42affa; font-size: 48px; width: 95%; line-height: 1.4;">
**How Evidence Accumulation Works:**
<br><br>
• **Start with Prior Belief**: P(Event) - our initial confidence before new evidence 
<br><br>
• **Update with Evidence**: Each new observation becomes "Evidence," and we set up a way of determining if this evidence is likely
<br><br>
• **Calculate New Confidence**: The posterior P(Event|Evidence) becomes our new prior for the next update
<br><br>
• **Iterative Process**: Previous posterior → new prior → collect evidence → update → repeat
<br><br>
This creates a **feedback loop** where reliable evidence strengthens our confidence, while contradictory evidence appropriately weakens it, leading to increasingly accurate beliefs over time.
</div>


:::

## Activity: Bayes and the Broken Motor

### Setup
* **Box A (Good Motor):** 36 Green beads (90%), 4 Red beads (10%)
* **Box B (Bad Motor):** 20 Green beads (50%), 20 Red beads (50%)
* Student draws a bead from a randomly chosen box.

### Scenario
Suppose a student draws a **red bead**. What is the probability it came from Box B?

### Bayes Calculation
$$
P(\text{Box B} \mid \text{Red}) = \frac{P(\text{Red} \mid \text{Box B}) \cdot P(\text{Box B})}{P(\text{Red})}
$$

## Activity: Bayes and the Broken Motor

**Step 1: Priors**  
$P(\text{Box A}) = 0.5$  
$P(\text{Box B}) = 0.5$

**Step 2: Likelihoods**  
$P(\text{Red} \mid \text{Box A}) = \frac{4}{40} = 0.10$  
$P(\text{Red} \mid \text{Box B}) = \frac{20}{40} = 0.50$

**Step 3: Total probability of red bead**  
$P(\text{Red}) = 0.10 \times 0.5 + 0.50 \times 0.5 = 0.05 + 0.25 = 0.30$

$$
P(\text{Box B} \mid \text{Red}) = \frac{P(\text{Red} \mid \text{Box B}) \cdot P(\text{Box B})}{P(\text{Red})}
$$


## Example Draw Sequences
```{python}
#| echo: false
#| eval: true
import pandas as pd
from IPython.display import display, Markdown

# Likelihoods
pRGB = 0.5  # P(Red | Box B)
pRGA = 0.1  # P(Red | Box A)
pGGB = 0.5  # P(Green | Box B)
pGGA = 0.9  # P(Green | Box A)

# Initial priors
pB_init = 0.5
pA_init = 0.5

sequence1 = ["r", "g", "r", "g"]
sequence2 = ["g", "g", "r", "g", "r"]
sequence3 = ["r", "r", "g", "r", "g"]

sequences = [
    ("Sequence 1", sequence1),
    ("Sequence 2", sequence2),
    ("Sequence 3", sequence3)
]

# Process all sequences and store results
all_results = []

for seq_name, sequence in sequences:
    pB = pB_init
    pA = pA_init
    
    results = [("Initial", "-", round(pB * 100, 1))]
    
    for i, color in enumerate(sequence, 1):
        if color == "r":
            # Red bead drawn
            likelihood_A = pRGA
            likelihood_B = pRGB
        else:
            # Green bead drawn
            likelihood_A = pGGA
            likelihood_B = pGGB
        
        # Calculate total probability of observing this color
        p_color = likelihood_A * pA + likelihood_B * pB
        
        # Update posteriors using Bayes' theorem
        pA = (likelihood_A * pA) / p_color
        pB = (likelihood_B * pB) / p_color
        
        results.append((f"Draw {i}", color.upper(), round(pB * 100, 1)))
    
    # Create DataFrame for this sequence
    df = pd.DataFrame(results, columns=['Step', 'Bead Color', f'P(Box B) % - {seq_name}'])
    all_results.append(df)

# Display in 3 columns using HTML
from IPython.display import HTML

# Convert DataFrames to HTML
html_tables = []
for df in all_results:
    html_table = df.to_html(index=False, table_id="bayesian-table", 
                           classes="table table-striped",
                           escape=False)
    html_tables.append(html_table)

# Create 3-column layout
html_output = f"""
<div style="display: flex; justify-content: space-between; gap: 20px;">
    <div style="flex: 1;">{html_tables[0]}</div>
    <div style="flex: 1;">{html_tables[1]}</div>
    <div style="flex: 1;">{html_tables[2]}</div>
</div>
"""

display(HTML(html_output))
```

**Notice:** Red beads increase P(Box B), green beads decrease it!

import numpy as np
from scipy.stats import norm

def generate_gaussian_svg(mu_px, sigma_px, data_id="bellcurve", 
                         svg_width=1500, svg_height=880,
                         color="#4296ff", fill_opacity=0.3):
    """
    Generate SVG element for a Gaussian/normal distribution curve.
    WITHOUT section wrapper for embedding in slides.
    """
    
    # Define x range
    x_min = 0
    x_max = svg_width
    baseline = svg_height - 50
    
    # FIXED number of points for consistent structure
    num_points = 100
    x_values = np.linspace(x_min, x_max, num_points)
    
    # Calculate y values using Gaussian formula
    peak_height = (40/sigma_px) * svg_height
    
    y_values = []
    for x in x_values:
        exponent = -((x - mu_px) ** 2) / (2 * sigma_px ** 2)
        y = np.exp(exponent)
        y_pixel = baseline - (y * peak_height)
        y_values.append(y_pixel)
    
    # Create points string for polyline
    points = " ".join([f"{x:.2f},{y:.2f}" for x, y in zip(x_values, y_values)])
    
    # Create points for filled polygon (add baseline corners)
    fill_points = points + f" {x_values[-1]:.2f},{baseline} {x_values[0]:.2f},{baseline}"
    
    # Generate SVG with RGB color conversion
    rgb = tuple(int(color.lstrip('#')[i:i+2], 16) for i in (0, 2, 4))
    fill_color = f"rgba({rgb[0]}, {rgb[1]}, {rgb[2]}, {fill_opacity})"
    
    # Return ONLY the SVG element, no section wrapper
    svg = f'''<svg data-id="{data_id}" style="position: absolute; left: 100px; top: 100px; width: {svg_width}px; height: {svg_height}px;">
  <polygon points="{fill_points}" 
           fill="{fill_color}" 
           stroke="{color}" 
           stroke-width="4"
           stroke-linejoin="round"/>
</svg>'''
    
    return svg

_generate_gaussian_svg = generate_gaussian_svg
```

#| echo: false
#| output: false

def generate_morph_slides(start_params, end_params, num_steps=10):
    """
    Generate intermediate slides for smooth morphing animation.
    
    start_params: dict with 'mu_px' and 'sigma_px' for starting positions
    end_params: dict with 'mu_px' and 'sigma_px' for ending positions
    num_steps: number of intermediate frames
    """
    slides = []
    
    for i in range(num_steps + 1):
        # Linear interpolation factor (0 to 1)
        t = i / num_steps
        
        # Interpolate parameters for both curves
        mu1 = start_params['curve1']['mu_px'] + t * (end_params['curve1']['mu_px'] - start_params['curve1']['mu_px'])
        sigma1 = start_params['curve1']['sigma_px'] + t * (end_params['curve1']['sigma_px'] - start_params['curve1']['sigma_px'])
        
        mu2 = start_params['curve2']['mu_px'] + t * (end_params['curve2']['mu_px'] - start_params['curve2']['mu_px'])
        sigma2 = start_params['curve2']['sigma_px'] + t * (end_params['curve2']['sigma_px'] - start_params['curve2']['sigma_px'])
        
        # Generate SVGs for this frame
        svg1 = _generate_gaussian_svg(mu_px=mu1, sigma_px=sigma1, svg_height=830, 
                                      data_id="bellcurve3", color="#55a709ff")
        svg2 = _generate_gaussian_svg(mu_px=mu2, sigma_px=sigma2, svg_height=830, 
                                      svg_width=1500, data_id="bellcurve4", color="#5178f8ff")
        
        slides.append((svg1, svg2))
    
    return slides

# Define start and end states
start_state = {
    'curve1': {'mu_px': 650, 'sigma_px': 150},
    'curve2': {'mu_px': 1000, 'sigma_px': 50}
}

end_state = {
    'curve1': {'mu_px': 900, 'sigma_px': 37},
    'curve2': {'mu_px': 900, 'sigma_px': 37}
}

# Generate 15 intermediate frames for smooth animation
morph_slides = generate_morph_slides(start_state, end_state, num_steps=15)
```
